bibliographic.title: The imperative for regulatory oversight of large language models (or generative AI) in healthcare
bibliographic.citation_apa: Meskó, B., & Topol, E. J. (2023). The imperative for regulatory oversight of large language models (or generative AI) in healthcare. npj Digital Medicine, 6, 120. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-023-00873-0

methodology.technology_context: GPT-4, Bard, ChatGPT; LLMs used as chatbots, clinical documentation tools, diagnostic assistants, and other healthcare applications

eligibility.decision_rationale: Perspective piece arguing for regulatory oversight of LLMs and generative AI in healthcare, with explicit discussion of conversational chatbots, safety, privacy, bias, and regulator-facing recommendations. Relevant as foundational policy context for governance in regulated healthcare, but not an empirical or operational study of conversational governance mechanisms.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only front matter and page 1 excerpt provided; full list of practical regulatory recommendations and depth of oversight mechanisms not visible in supplied text.

appraisal.notes: Normative perspective appropriate to its policy aim, but lacks empirical sampling, data collection, or evaluative methods. Appraisal reflects argument quality and clarity rather than empirical rigor.

cerqual.explanation: The argument is coherent and directly relevant to LLM governance in regulated healthcare, including chatbot use cases, but confidence is moderated because the supplied text is a perspective without empirical validation and the full recommendation set is incomplete in the excerpt.

coding.theme: Regulatory oversight of LLMs in healthcare
coding.subtheme: Policy recommendations and risk framing for regulators

synthesis.main_claim: LLMs and generative AI in healthcare require timely regulatory oversight so clinicians and patients can use them without harm, ethical compromise, or privacy loss, while preserving transformative potential.
synthesis.contribution: Frames why LLMs differ from already regulated medical AI, maps healthcare use cases including patient-facing chatbots, and outlines practical expectations for regulators.
synthesis.limitations: Perspective without empirical evaluation; supplied excerpt does not show explicit author-stated study limitations or complete recommendation detail.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational contextual evidence on macro-level regulatory governance of LLM-based conversational and clinical tools in healthcare; not central evidence for operational conversational governance such as guardrails, tracing, handoff, or post-deployment monitoring.

evidence.claim: Article is a peer-reviewed journal perspective on LLM regulatory oversight in healthcare.
evidence.excerpt: PERSPECTIVE OPEN The imperative for regulatory oversight of large language models (or generative AI) in healthcare

evidence.claim: Specific LLMs and conversational chatbot applications in healthcare are discussed.
evidence.excerpt: sophisticated large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 and Bard

evidence.claim: Chatbots are an explicit healthcare application of LLMs.
evidence.excerpt: working as a chatbot to answer questions for patients about their specific data and concerns

evidence.claim: Authors argue for regulatory oversight to prevent harm and protect privacy.

evidence.claim: Paper offers practical recommendations for regulators.
evidence.excerpt: This paper summarizes our practical recommendations for what we can expect from regulators to bring this vision to reality

evidence.claim: Regulation must address safety, ethics, bias, and privacy in healthcare LLM use.

evidence.claim: LLMs differ materially from already regulated AI-based medical technologies.
evidence.excerpt: LLMs warrant a very cautious approach since these models are trained differently from AI-based medical technologies that are regulated already

evidence.claim: A regulatory gap exists for NLP tokenization in healthcare.
evidence.excerpt: Tokenization is a crucial step in natural language processing (NLP) ... Currently, tokenization is not covered by healthcare regulators
